doc.title: Tom Albert and Milton "Mooney" Martin Interview, 1964-12-21

title: Dancing in the old days: no singing, quadrilles at eleven
summary: Martin says dancers recognized a schottische, waltz or two-step at once, and bands did not sing except when asked for a song, then played it twice. Tom adds that the quadrille came on around eleven o'clock, followed by a mazurka.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Well we still got another minute or so on here Mooney. I wonder if you can tell us anything about the dancing since you didn't play anything... Anything special about the dancing in the old days? Was it much different? I mean the steps and... Oh yeah. Faster, slower, what would you say?

Well now, the people played dance music... Yeah. In them days. If they played one of the dancers' sharders, they played a sharders. Well you don't dance a sharders. No sooner they bust out with it, you know it was a sharders or waltz or two-step or any of them kind. You dancing. Now you take for singing, the musicians didn't sing. No.
They didn't sing. No singing with the band.
No singing with the band. Only singing you had if a lady, a man, he said play me this and such a piece of my singing.
But they'd sing it. No. They'd sing it and then do the... We'll play it. Play it twice, they'd sing it.
Would they dance while they sang too or just stop and listen? Oh yeah. They'd dance.
They'd dance. They'd dance. And all about eleven o'clock, that's the time they'd play the uh, eleven o'clock they'd play the quadrille. Yeah. You know that? The quadrille?
